query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor Nb alloying addition (approximately 1–2 at%) to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy will refine its microstructure and promote additional ductile deformation mechanisms (such as enhanced nano‐twinning or dislocation interactions), thereby improving load‐bearing integrity (reducing cracking) without significantly impairing its large magneto- and pressure–caloric responses.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy that exhibits strong caloric responses under applied magnetic and pressure fields but suffers from poor load‐bearing integrity and a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Introduce 1–2 at% Nb into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Under operating conditions typical for solid refrigeration: the same applied magnetic fields, pressure fields, temperature ranges, and mechanical loading conditions as currently used.
generation.structural_mediator: Refinement of grain boundaries and promotion of nano‐twinning (or similar ductility‐enhancing microstructural features) that reduce crack initiation and propagation.
generation.mechanism: The Nb addition is expected to adjust the stacking fault energy and enhance microstructural features that are known to promote deformation twinning and dislocation mobility. This leads to improved ductility and fracture toughness (increased load-bearing integrity) while preserving the crucial caloric phase transitions responsible for the refrigerant performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: An alloy with enhanced mechanical integrity (evidenced by increased fracture toughness and reduced cracking) while maintaining its high magneto- and pressure–caloric effects with little to no degradation in caloric performance relative to the original alloy.
generation.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy shows high caloric responses under applied field and pressure operation but fails mechanically due to poor load-bearing behavior and crack propagation.
generation.boundary: The intervention remains applicable within the same applied magnetic and pressure fields, temperature ranges, and mechanical loading conditions as those used in existing refrigeration cycles.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Nb concentration and processing parameters may require fine-tuning to achieve the desired balance; it is uncertain whether a 1–2 at% addition will be fully adequate under all operational stress states without any slight compromise of caloric performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one with the standard (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 composition and another with 1–2 at% Nb added. Process both identically. Conduct mechanical tests (tensile, fracture toughness, and crack propagation studies) as well as measurements of caloric response (assessing magneto- and pressure–caloric effects) under the same magnetic, pressure, temperature, and loading conditions.
measurements: Fracture toughness and tensile strength (for load‐bearing integrity)
Crack frequency and propagation behavior (via microscopy)
Caloric response metrics (e.g., isothermal entropy change, adiabatic temperature change)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., fracture toughness or reduced cracking) or if its caloric response is significantly diminished (e.g., more than a 10% reduction) compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While the yield strength and KJIc fracture toughness of the medium-entropy CrCoNi and high-entropy CrMnFeCoNi alloys are comparable, the tensile strengths, tensile ductility and work of fracture of the CrCoNi alloy are significantly higher, by respectively ∼15, ∼30 and ∼50%, at room temperature. At cryogenic temperatures, the strengths of the two alloys are comparable (σUTS∼1,300 MPa at 77 K), but the KJIc fracture toughness, tensile ductility and work of fracture are again markedly higher in the CrCoNi alloy, by ∼25, ∼27 and ∼31%, respectively. The yield strength, σy, at 77 K is slightly below that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, which we believe is due to the non-uniform grain size of our present material (Fig. 1b–d). Consistent with this notion, in a previous study where the grain size of CrCoNi was uniform and comparable to that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, the tensile properties of the three-component alloy were found to exceed those of the five-component alloy at all temperatures.

These alloys can display excellent strength, ductility and toughness at room temperature, properties which are further enhanced or maintained at cryogenic temperatures where deformation nano-twinning becomes a more prominent mode of deformation. Despite our recent observations of various toughening mechanisms occurring on the nanometre length-scale in the vicinity of a crack tip in such an alloy, the quantitative strengthening effect from deformation twinning and the nature of twinning-induced plasticity remain somewhat uncertain. decision.trend: Early studies on related multi‐component alloys have shown that modest compositional tweaks (for example, additions of Si, C, or interstitial elements like N and C) can substantially improve mechanical robustness by refining microstructures, increasing hardness, and tailoring the stacking fault energy. Over time, researchers moved from simply characterizing the high caloric responses to engineering composition to enable mechanisms such as twin-boundary strengthening and transformation-induced toughening. However, while these interventions have yielded alloys with improved ductility and damage tolerance, the challenge of preserving the functional caloric phase transitions in the same operating magnetic and pressure regimes remains unsolved.
decision.unsolved: The open issue is how to enhance the load‐bearing integrity (i.e. reduce cracking) without impairing the large caloric responses observed in the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy. Prior work in similar high‐entropy systems has not yet demonstrated a minimal intervention that secures mechanical durability under the same applied magnetic/pressure conditions and temperature ranges.
decision.lever: minor alloying addition of ~1–2 at% Nb
decision.why: A small Nb addition is a logical next step because it follows a proven trend in high-/medium‐entropy alloy research where minimal compositional tuning improves mechanical integrity by refining the microstructure and promoting ductile deformation mechanisms (e.g., by modifying twin formation or dislocation interactions) without significantly altering the caloric phase transition. This approach precisely targets the niche of poor load‐bearing integrity while retaining the required magnetocaloric and pressure–caloric performance under the same operating conditions.
